title: Creative Environments
blurb: Describe your impressions of a place

steps.html:
One company will have your shirts washed and your car serviced so that you never leave the building. Another took its walls down and watched conversation fall by seventy per cent. Two texts that disagree, and one grammar point about getting things done for you.

  • Read two texts that argue against each other
  • Use have and get something done
  • Describe your impressions of a place
  • Write about the workspace you would design

To put power back into a battery; also, to rest and recover energy.
An extra benefit that comes with a job, beyond the salary.
To put something carefully in a particular position.
Useful and sensible in real situations.
To behave towards someone in a certain way; to give medical care; something special.
To cause something to start, especially an idea or a reaction.
Requiring no thought; done without thinking.
New and different from anything before; also, the first version.
For one particular purpose. Compare especially = above all.

steps.title: Before you read: what do you think perks are actually for?
The office with a slide in it
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 148 words

At the best-known technology campuses you can have your dry-cleaning collected from your desk, get your car serviced while you work, and have your teeth checked without leaving the building. There are ping-pong tables. In two offices there is a slide.

The argument behind the perks is not that they are fun. It is that anything taking an employee out of the building is a cost, and that anything which can be done for them should be. A person who has their shirts washed for them works two more hours a week.

The second argument is about collisions. Long tables, open kitchens and a swing in the corridor are designed to make people bump into each other, on the theory that ideas are sparked by conversations nobody planned.

It is a serious idea dressed up as a childish one, which is why it is so easy to make fun of.

steps.title: Or: give people a door that shuts
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 148 words

The research on open offices is not kind to them. When one large company had its walls taken down and its desks rearranged into rows, face-to-face conversation fell by seventy per cent and email rose. The collisions happened; people simply avoided them.

The counter-argument is not that offices should be dull. It is that concentration is the scarce resource, and that a decorated lamp post is no substitute for a room with a door.

There is a version of the perks argument that survives this. Having your admin done for you is genuinely useful, and so is having your cleaning done at night. A ping-pong table is not, unless you wanted one.

The most user-friendly office anybody has described is dull, quiet, and arranged so that nobody has their concentration broken and nobody has to get their real work done at home.

steps.title: have / get + object + past participle
steps.html:
The structure for things you arrange rather than do.

When somebody else does something for you, English does not usually name them. It uses have or get + the thing + past participle: I had my car serviced. You can get your dry-cleaning done.

The word order matters. The object comes before the participle: have your shirts washed, never have washed your shirts. That second order would mean you did it.

Have and get are almost interchangeable here. Get is slightly more informal, and slightly more likely when you had to arrange it yourself.

Both work in every tense, because it is have or get that carries it: I have it done / I had it done / I am having it done / I will have it done / I have had it done.

There is a second, unhappier use. Have something done also describes something bad that happened to you: She had her bag stolen on the train. She did not arrange that.

Finally, get someone to do something is different: it means persuading a person. I got my brother to fix it — a person, an infinitive. I got it fixed — a thing, a participle.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts and around them.

You can have your dry-cleaning collected from your desk.
Arranged for you.

You can get your car serviced while you work.
Get, informal, same meaning.

You can have a health check without leaving the building.
No participle needed — check is a noun here.

A person who has their shirts washed works two more hours a week.
Object before the participle.

One company had its walls taken down.
Past tense on have.

Having your admin done for you is genuinely useful.
The whole structure as a subject.

I'm having the kitchen painted next week.
Continuous, for an arrangement.

We will have the report translated by Friday.
Future.

She had her bag stolen on the train.
The unhappy use — nobody arranged this.

I got my brother to fix the tap.
A person + infinitive: persuading.

I got the tap fixed.
A thing + participle: arranging.

I had washed my shirts
Different meaning entirely: you washed them.

steps.title: Three sentences that look the same and are not
steps.html:
1. Fact: your car needed servicing, and a garage did it.
  2. You did not do it, and you arranged it: I had my car serviced. Object my car, then the participle serviced.
  3. Now change the order: I had serviced my car is a past perfect and means you had already serviced it yourself. Same words, opposite meaning.
  4. Now the person: I got my brother to service it. Person + to + infinitive, because you persuaded somebody.
  5. And the unhappy version: I had my car stolen last week. Nobody arranged that; the structure simply reports something done to you.

steps.title: You are going to describe the workspace you would design.

options.label: Perks and collisions — the first text is right
Doors and quiet — the second text is right
Neither: describe what you would actually build

steps.title: Write your description.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Say what would be provided, what would be arranged for people, and what you would leave out. Use the causative at least four times.
steps.html:
• Open with what your workspace would look like.
  • Say what would be arranged for people, using <i>have / get something done</i>.
  • Say what you would leave out, and why.
  • Close with the one rule the whole design follows.

Useful language

  • You would be able to have your … done / collected / arranged.
  • Nobody would have to get their … fixed in their own time.
  • What I would not have installed is …
  • The point is not to … but to …
  • Concentration is the scarce resource, not …
  • It would be dull to look at, and that is the point.
steps.modelHtml:
The building I would put people in

It would be dull to look at, and that would be the point. No slide, no swing, and nothing painted a colour anybody would photograph.

What I would keep is the part of the argument that actually works. You would be able to have your admin done for you, get your prescriptions collected, and have a health check without taking a morning off. All of those remove an interruption. Nobody would have to get anything fixed in their own time.

What I would not have installed is a ping-pong table. If two people want a conversation, they can have one; a table in the corridor does not create ideas, it creates noise for the fourteen people who did not want to join in.

Everyone would have a door. That is the entire design.
